definition: A family of sulfur-rich structural proteins that make up wool, hair and horn; in textile fibers it forms alpha-helical filaments embedded in a protein matrix cross-linked by cystine disulfide bonds.
explanation: Wool and specialty hair fibers are built from trichocyte, or hard, keratins. Type I and type II keratin chains each have a central alpha-helical rod flanked by non-helical head and tail domains. Two helices wind together into a coiled-coil dimer, and dimers assemble through protofilaments into intermediate filaments about 10 nanometers across. Bundles of these filaments are embedded in a matrix of keratin-associated proteins, some very rich in cysteine and others rich in glycine and tyrosine. Disulfide bonds between cysteine residues, which together form cystine, tie filaments and matrix into a network that resists solvents and gives wool its resilience.
example: A tailor steams and presses a crease into wool trousers, and the crease lasts through many wearings, while an unpressed wool sleeve slowly relaxes on a humid day. The class uses this to show that keratin's shape is held by bonds that can be loosened and re-formed: moisture and heat free the structure to take a new form, and cooling and drying fix it in place until moisture releases it again.
caution: Keratin is a protein family, not a single molecule. Different species, and different regions within one fiber, contain different mixtures of keratins and associated proteins. The soft keratins of skin differ from the hard keratins of fibers. Products described as keratin treatments usually contain hydrolyzed protein fragments, which do not rebuild the native filament structure. The word alone says nothing about fineness, softness or animal welfare.
deeper: The alpha-helix proposed by Pauling, Corey and Branson in 1951 has about 3.6 amino acid residues per turn and a pitch of about 0.54 nm; in keratin, helices from type I and type II chains wind around one another as coiled coils. Stretching moist wool or hair converts part of this structure toward an extended beta form, a change first recorded by X-ray diffraction in the early 1930s. Hard keratins are cysteine-rich, and the density of disulfide cross-links governs their compactness and insolubility: they dissolve in ordinary protein solvents only at pH extremes or after the disulfides are chemically reduced. Within a wool fiber the paracortex is richer in high-sulfur proteins, while the orthocortex carries more low-sulfur and glycine-rich proteins, a compositional difference linked to crimp.
origins: The name derives from the Greek keras, horn. In the early 1930s William Astbury's X-ray diffraction studies of wool and hair identified two distinct states, which he called alpha-keratin and beta-keratin; the alpha and beta labels were later adopted for protein secondary structure generally. The alpha-helix itself was proposed in 1951, and models in which helices twist around each other as compound or coiled coils to explain alpha-keratin followed in the 1950s and 1960s.

definition: A standardized method for quantifying the environmental impacts of a product across its life stages, from raw material extraction through production, use and disposal.
explanation: An LCA starts by defining its goal, scope and functional unit, such as one kilogram of spun yarn or one garment worn a given number of times. It then compiles a life cycle inventory of inputs and outputs, including energy, water, chemicals and emissions, within stated system boundaries. The impact assessment converts those flows into indicators such as climate change, water scarcity or eutrophication, and the interpretation phase examines uncertainty, sensitivity and limits. The international framework is set out in ISO 14040 and ISO 14044.
example: Two studies compare cotton and polyester T-shirts and reach opposite conclusions. A student reading them should check the functional unit, whether use-phase washing is included, which regions' farming or electricity data were used, how co-products such as cottonseed were allocated, and which impact categories were reported. Different choices can legitimately produce different answers, which is why method disclosure matters.
caution: An LCA result is conditional on its boundaries, data and assumptions; it is not a single objective score for a fiber. Cradle-to-gate studies omit use and end of life, and many studies leave out biodiversity, microplastic release, animal welfare or social impacts. Comparative public claims deserve more scrutiny, including independent review, than internal screening studies.
deeper: Inventory data come from primary measurements or background databases, and allocation rules split burdens among co-products, such as lint and seed at the gin or wool and meat on a farm. Characterization multiplies each flow by a factor, such as a global warming potential, and sums results per impact category. A systematic review of textile LCAs found that production and use phases carry the largest share of impacts while end of life usually contributes little, and noted a paucity of studies comparing different fibers for the same functional unit. A review of reuse and recycling LCAs found results most sensitive to recycling yields, use-phase variables and assumptions about which virgin production is displaced, and found that practices extending service life gave the lowest impacts.
origins: According to a review in Environmental Science and Technology, life cycle work grew during the 1970s from energy analyses of products into comprehensive environmental burden analysis. Full impact assessment and life cycle costing models followed in the 1980s and 1990s, and social and consequential LCA gained ground in the 2000s. The ISO 14040 series gave practitioners a shared framework, and fashion-sector reviews now examine both the value and the limits of LCA for guiding company decisions.
